cues.text: Section seven: the GlobalCare case, and how it connects to the continuous assessment application.
Let's begin with GlobalCare.
This organisation operates in more than 25 countries.
Its original design placed everything in one central European database, and that choice produced four problems.
First, latency: users in Africa and Asia were far from the central database, so their requests were slow.
Second, scaling problems, because one central system had to carry the load of the whole world.
Third, failures that affected global service, meaning that when the central database had trouble, users everywhere felt it.
And fourth, localisation concerns, which means the needs and rules of individual regions were not well served by a single European location.
The recommended response has several parts.
Use regional partitions for records where appropriate, so that data sits in the region it mainly belongs to.
Provide local access with replication for availability, so that users reach nearby copies and the service stays up if one site fails.
Add a controlled global directory and routing layer, so the system knows where each record lives and sends requests to the right place.
And use strong coordination for critical updates, so that the most important changes are made consistently.
By contrast, noncritical reporting can tolerate asynchronous replication, which means copies may lag slightly behind and that is acceptable for reports.

The source also lists things that must be planned: identity resolution, so the same person or entity is recognised across regions; encryption; audited access, so you can see who accessed what; recovery tests, so you know restoration actually works; and compliant transfers when data crosses borders.
Then comes an important warning.
Never claim that local storage alone ensures regulatory compliance.
Keeping data in a country is not, by itself, enough.
Next, the fifth component of the completed CA portfolio.
It examines distributed and cloud architecture.
The source notes that its historical local inspection showed a PostgreSQL primary without a replica.
So you must distinguish an architecture proposal from deployed evidence.
What was observed is a primary with no replica; anything beyond that is a proposal.
In the portfolio you should explain three things: how a standby would be configured, how lag would be measured, and how failover would be tested.
You must do this without inventing replication results, because no replica was actually shown to exist.
Now the VitalNet lab.
The scenario is that Enugu clinics require access during a broken link to Kano.
The lab asks you to do the following.
Partition patient and visit rows by region.
Simulate local routing.
Simulate an unreachable remote node.
Then verify that Enugu queries still return locally held records.
What does this demonstrate?
It demonstrates the idea of locality and partial availability.
It is not a formal proof that a production system is AP, that is, availability-favouring under partition.
You must also define which operations must stop when the link fails, and how conflicts are reconciled afterwards.
Now two essay topics.
The first essay: discuss CAP and consistency choices for a healthcare system.
You should define C, A and P precisely.
Show a network split, where the system is divided and parts cannot communicate.

Explain the CP response and the AP response: a CP response favours consistency and may refuse some requests during the split, while an AP response keeps serving requests and may return data that is not fully up to date.
Then make a choice: use strong coordination for critical clinical changes, and carefully bounded staleness for noncritical data, meaning data may be out of date, but only within limits you define.
Finally, discuss reconciliation, recovery and legal constraints.
The second essay: compare fragmentation and replication.
The core distinction is that fragmentation divides data, while replication duplicates it.
Explain horizontal, vertical and hybrid fragmentation, each with reconstruction examples, that is, how the original table is rebuilt from its pieces.
Compare synchronous and asynchronous copies.
Assess latency, redundancy, storage, write overhead and failure tolerance.
Conclude with a workload-driven hybrid design, one chosen according to how the system is actually used.
Finally, the closing heading of this chapter: GlobalCare case details and additional comparison.
That is the theme tying these pieces together: one global case, and a careful comparison of how data can be split and copied across places.
